chunks.input: TITLE: Manipulating aspen ( Populus tremuloides ) seedling size characteristics to improve initial establishment and growth on competitive sites SPECIES: T1=Populus tremuloides (aspen, aspen seedlings); T2=Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle, forbs); T3=Pinus contorta (pine seedlings); T4=Pinus halepensis (pine seedlings); T5=Melilotus officinalis; T6=Alopecurus aequalis; T7=Bromus ciliatus; T8=Bromus inermis; T9=Medicago sativa; T10=Phalaris arundinacea; T11=Poa pratensis CONTEXT: In this paper, we evaluated the effect of size and root-toshoot ratio on the early establishment of aspen seedlings after outplanting over a range of field conditions that varied in the amount and type of competition, as well as in edaphic conditions. The styroblock containers were composed of a polystyrene foam block with a series of cells which varied by diameter instead of depth for each specific container size, allowing a similar root structure to be maintained between treatments. Afterwards seedlings were moved outside for the rest of the growing season (with earlier sow dates moved out first). Bud set occurred approximately two weeks after treatment. After complete leaf senescence occurred (November 1), seedlings were lifted, packaged into cardboard boxes with plastic liners and placed into frozen storage (−4°C) until outplanting in the spring of 2014. At the time of fall lifting, a representative subset of 10 seedlings from several size classes were subsampled to determine initial morphological traits. Height and root collar diameter were measured, and roots and stems were separated for their respective dry mass measurements from which root-to-shoot ratios were calculated (Table 1). It should be noted that a root-to-shoot ratio of 1.60 can be considered high, relative to commercial seedling stock that has been produced in the recent past (root-to-shoot ratio of control seedlings previously produced by [ref] as low as 0.8). In the spring of 2014, seedlings were outplanted into two study areas. The first study area was comprised of three separate and independent sites at the Crop Diversification Center North (hereafter, CDC), a large agricultural research facility in the parkland region of Alberta (Edmonton, Alberta 53.642, -113.361; elevation 651 m a.s.l.) (Table 2). TEXT: [1] (abs) Trembling aspen is an important component of the boreal mixedwood forest region and is a key component of numerous ecological functions. [2] (abs) As a result, aspen has become a target species for forest restoration after industrial disturbance; however, aspen seedling afforestation research is still in its infancy as seedling and site characteristics and their interactions which drive establishment success in the field are poorly understood. [3] (abs) This study examined the growth response of three aspen size classes across six sites differing in competition and soil moisture availability. [4] (abs) With competing vegetation present, tall seedlings with lower root-to-shoot ratios had less height growth aboveground and reduced root egress (relative to total root mass) belowground, indicating that light was not the most limiting factor aboveground and that higher root-to-shoot ratios may aid in competition for rooting space. [5] (abs) Differences between size classes were less pronounced on sites with no competition or sites with extreme conditions (high competition or low soil moisture availability) during outplanting. [6] (abs) Reducing competing vegetation before outplanting improved height growth, particularly in seedlings with high root-to-shoot ratios. [7] (abs) For aspen, planting short to medium-sized seedlings with higher root-to-shoot ratios offers a reasonable balance between cost and production of a stress-tolerant seedling. [8] (abs) Root-to-shoot ratio; grass competition; seedling quality; soil moisture availability; forest restoration [9] (res) The weather conditions for the duration of the experiment and between the two study areas were mainly driven by differences in precipitation, where the CDC sites in Edmonton had greater summer precipitation and were warmer relative to the sites in the Peace River region (Figure 1(a); Appendix 1, 5). [10] (res) Overall, the weather was colder and wetter during the year of establishment (2014) and warmer and drier in the second year (2015). [11] (res) A 10-year climate average (2004–2013) preceding the year of establishment did not reveal any adverse conditions during the year of planting however, large inter-annual fluctuations in weather were present. [12] (res) Edaphic conditions varied somewhat among the three CDC sites, where soil texture ranged from a sandy loam to clay loam. [13] (res) The Mulch site had higher soil bulk density and soil temperature compared to the other two sites (Grass and Plow); the warmer soil temperature in the Mulch site was likely due to the exposed black plastic mulch warming the ground, whereas the other CDC sites had dense coverage of vegetation insulating the soil. [14] (res) Monthly volumetric water content was significantly lower in the Mulch and was highest in the Grass site, with the Plow site falling in-between. [15] (res) Some soil macronutrients (NH4, K, S, Mg) were lower in the Mulch site relative to the Plow and Grass site. [16] (res) For the Peace River sites, the Gravel-pit had the highest sand content resulting in a loam soil texture compared to silty clay loam soil textures for the Aq-field and Well-site. [17] (res) Soil bulk density was very similar among sites, however the Gravel-pit site had high soil compaction at the lower soil depths (>1.6 g cm-3). [18] (res) Monthly volumetric water content over the growing season was less than half in the Gravel-pit planting site compared to the Ag-field and the Well-site, however, water content decreased both in the Well-site and Gravel-pit later in the growing season. [19] (res) Seasonal soil temperature was highest at the Ag-field. [20] (res) Soil macronutrient concentrations in surface soils varied among the Peace River sites, but there was no systematic trend (i.e. no site that clearly had lower overall soil nutrient concentrations) [21] (res) The type of competition among sites (above and belowground) was highly variable (Figure 1(b)); however, the principal component analysis also showed a positive correlation between root mass with grass cover and between forb mass and the height of the competing vegetation. [22] (res) The Pearson correlation coefficients for these relationships were both significant with r = 0.95 and r = 0.92, respectively. [23] (res) On the extremes, the Well-site was dominated by forbs (predominantly Melilotus officinalis (L.) Pall.), the Gravel-pit by grass cover (predominantly Bromus ciliatus L.) and the Ag-field with the least amount of grass cover. [24] (res) The CDC sites tended to have a mixture of forbs (Cirsium arvense (L.) Scop. dominant on the Plow site and Medicago sativa L. dominant on the Grass site) and grasses (primarily Alopecurus aequalis Sobol., Bromus inermis Leyss., Phalaris arundinacea L., and Poa pratensis L) with vegetation cover values inside the extremes observed on the Peace River sites. [25] (res) Survival at all sites was generally very high (75% to 100%). [26] (res) The highest mortality was observed in the Plow and Gravel-pit sites, specifically for the tall seedlings at the [27] (res) Figure 2. [28] (res) Least squares means of seedling aboveground growth characteristics for size class, site, and study area; (a) initial height in 2014, (b) 2-year growth increment after growing season 2014/15, and (c) total height in 2015. [29] (res) Error bars represent the 95% confidence interval (n = 10). [30] (res) Lettering indicates significant differences for significant interaction term within each sub-panel (Tukey-adjusted). [31] (res) In cases where the interaction is not significant refer to Table 5 for significant main effects. [32] (res) Short = Short seedlings; Medium = Medium tall seedlings; Tall = Tall seedlings. [33] (res) Gravel-pit site (median value = 75%, Table 4). [34] (res) Short seedlings tended to have the highest survival with four of the six sites showing 100% survival with exception of the most extreme sites (Grass site at CDC and Gravel-pit in Peace River, Table 4). [35] (res) However, these differences could not be tested statistically since the logistic regression analysis resulted in complete separation (see Materials and Methods section for details). [36] (res) At the time of planting the height of seedlings in the tall size class was over three times that of the medium and short size class (Figure 2(a)). [37] (res) Initial seedling height had a strong influence on subsequent height growth. [38] (res) On four out of the six sites (Mulch, Plow, Ag-field, Well-site) short size class seedlings grew more in height (height increment) than the tall size class over the two growing seasons (Figure 2(b)) while the medium size class grew more on half the sites. [39] (res) After two growing seasons, the initial height advantage of the tall size class was reduced to 30–40% (Figure 2(c)). [40] (res) When separating the growth of seedlings by growing season, short and medium seedlings had greater growth in the first growing season (2014) compared to the tall seedling size class; however, in the second growing season height growth was similar among the size classes. [41] (res) Total leaf mass was highest on sites with less competing vegetation (Mulch and Ag-field) and the tall size class seedlings had greater leaf mass than the shorter seedlings across sites (except on the Gravel-pit) (Figure 4(a)). [42] (res) There was no difference in specific leaf area between sites or size classes at CDC; however, specific leaf area was lowest at the Ag-field (Figure 4(b)) [43] (res) Figure 3. [44] (res) Least squares means of aspen height growth for size class, site, year, and study area. [45] (res) Error bars represent the 95% confidence interval (n = 10). [46] (res) Lettering indicates significant differences for significant interaction term within each sub-panel (Tukey-adjusted). [47] (res) In cases where the interaction is not significant refer to Table 5 for significant main effects. [48] (res) Short = Short seedlings; Medium = Medium tall seedlings; Tall = Tall seedlings. [49] (res) Overall, the tall size class had significantly more root growth than the short size class in the Mulch and Grass sites (CDC) as well as the Ag-field and Well-site (Peace River study area) (Figure 5(a)). [50] (res) However, proportionally the relative increase in total root mass was often (though dependent on the site) greatest (four time increase from initial conditions) in the shortest size class relative to the medium and tall size class, where root mass was only 2.2-2.5 times greater after two years. [51] (res) Root growth was proportional to total root mass, as tall seedlings showed greater root growth relative to small seedlings at each site (Figure 5(b)). [52] (res) Root-to-shoot ratios after two growing seasons were very similar among size classes with most of the differences occurring among sites, except for the Grass and Gravel-pit sites where the short size class continued to have significantly higher root-to-shoot ratios relative to the tall size class (Figure 5(c)). [53] (res) Seedlings in the Mulch site (least competition) showed the lowest root-to-shoot ratios of all sites (Figure 5(c)). [54] (res) Comparing the three sites at CDC, the percent root egress was highest in the Mulch (least competition). [55] (res) Between the Peace River sites, the level of root egress was extremely low at the Gravel-pit relative to the other sites; it is notable that the short size class showed the greatest root egress (relative to total root mass) on both the Ag-field and Well-site (Figure 5(d)). [56] (res) Figure 4. [57] (res) Least squares means of aspen seedling leaf measures for different size classes, sites, and study area in the second growing season; (a) total leaf mass and (b) specific leaf area. [58] (res) All measurements were taken in 2015. [59] (res) Error bars represent the 95% confidence interval (n = 10). [60] (res) Lettering indicates significant differences for significant interaction term within each sub-panel (Tukey-adjusted). [61] (res) In cases where the interaction is not significant refer to Table 5 for significant main effects. [62] (res) Short = Short seedlings; Medium = Medium tall seedlings; Tall = Tall seedlings.

The styroblock containers were composed of a polystyrene foam block with a series of cells which varied by diameter instead of depth for each specific container size, allowing a similar root structure to be maintained between treatments. Afterwards seedlings were moved outside for the rest of the growing season (with earlier sow dates moved out first). Bud set occurred approximately two weeks after treatment. It should be noted that a root-to-shoot ratio of 1.60 can be considered high, relative to commercial seedling stock that has been produced in the recent past (root-to-shoot ratio of control seedlings previously produced by [ref] as low as 0.8). In the spring of 2014, seedlings were outplanted into two study areas. The first study area was comprised of three separate and independent sites at the Crop Diversification Center North (hereafter, CDC), a large agricultural research facility in the parkland region of Alberta (Edmonton, Alberta 53.642, -113.361; elevation 651 m a.s.l.) (Table 2). TEXT: [63] (dis) Regardless of the degree and composition of vegetation competition, the potential advantage of using a taller aspen seedling did not result in greater overall growth benefits (in the first 2 years) relative to using the short and medium-sized seedlings. [64] (dis) This response may be at least partly attributable to morphological differences between the tall and short seedling size classes, including higher initial root-to-shoot ratios, that might have allowed for greater root egress into the surrounding soil providing more water for shoot and leaf expansion. [65] (dis) High initial root-to-shoot ratios have been previously shown to result in greater height growth (Martens et al. 2007; Landhäusser et al. 2012a; Landhäusser et al. 2012b), while greater transpirational demand placed on taller seedlings (with more leaf area and lower root-to-shoot ratio) planted into a stressful environment may have further contributed to reduced shoot extension. [66] (dis) Seedling size classes had similar specific leaf area within each site in both study areas; however, seedlings in the tall size class typically had greater total leaf mass (excluding Ag-field and Gravel-pit). [67] (dis) This would suggest that total leaf area was higher in taller seedlings, resulting in greater transpirational demand. [68] (dis) When faced with aboveground competition, aspen seedlings tend to prioritize shoot growth. [69] (dis) In our study, shoot growth appeared to be prioritized in the shorter seedlings potentially to prevent them from being shaded out, while taller seedlings were less directly affected by aboveground competition and as a result prioritized carbon allocation to other parts of the plant. [70] (dis) In fact, greater total root growth was found in taller seedlings in all sites except the Gravel-pit (Figure 5(b)). [71] (dis) The tall seedlings also had initially larger root systems with a greater NSC reserve pool, which could have supported higher root growth (Figure 5(b)). [72] (dis) In addition, light availability has been shown to be an important factor for improving root development of aspen seedlings (Landhäusser and Lieffers 2001; Kelly et al. 2015). [73] (dis) Increased water stress (from belowground competition) may also be a contributing factor towards increased root growth for improving internal water balance, responses similar to those were found in Aleppo pine seedlings (Pinus halepensis Mill.) planted with and without competition. [74] (dis) Figure 5. [75] (dis) Least squares means of aspen seedling belowground measures for different size classes, sites, and study area after two growing seasons; (a) root mass, (b) root growth, (c) root to shoot ratio, and (d) root egress. [76] (dis) All measurements were taken in 2015. [77] (dis) Error bars represent the 95% confidence interval (n = 10). [78] (dis) Lettering indicates significant differences for significant interaction term within each sub-panel (Tukey-adjusted). [79] (dis) In cases where the interaction is not significant refer to Table 5 for significant main effects. [80] (dis) Short = Short seedlings; Medium = Medium tall seedlings; Tall = Tall seedlings. [81] (dis) Competition removal prior to planting appeared to benefit the short and medium-size classes, which showed greater first-year height increment over tall size class seedlings with low root-to-shoot ratios. [82] (dis) Although these plants were smaller, their higher root-to-shoot ratios were likely beneficial in the development of vigorous shoot growth. [83] (dis) In aspen, high root-to-shoot ratios are often a good indicator of carbon storage reserves (Landhäusser et al. 2012a). [84] (dis) At each of these sites (Plow, Well-site), vegetation competition was removed temporarily following site preparation allowing shorter seedlings with a high root-to-shoot ratio to grow faster. [85] (dis) However, this window of opportunity was short-lived, as in the following year, competing vegetation recovered rapidly with different grasses and tall weedy forbs such as sweet clover (Melilotus officinalis (L.) Pall.) and Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense (L.) Scop.) proliferating. [86] (dis) The rapid development of competing vegetation depressed height increment of short and medium-sized seedlings in the second year, leading to similar second year height growth for all three size classes. [87] (dis) Despite this, total growth increment over the two-year period was still significantly greater in the short size class relative to tall size class on both the Plow and Well-site due to differences in root-toshoot ratio, further illustrating the influence of initial morphology of seedling stock on initial establishment. [88] (dis) Achieving early canopy closure is a management strategy for controlling competing vegetation in forest restoration and is driven by factors such as species composition, planting density, and early growth. [89] (dis) Regardless of these drivers, early seedling growth is crucial and may require the management or control of vegetation beyond the first year, especially on very competitive sites. [90] (dis) While tall size class seedlings maintained their height advantage at every site, a tall shoot was not critical to the growth of aspen on sites with favorable growing conditions (i.e. the Mulch site). [91] (dis) The difference in total height (i.e. height advantage) of the tall size class was drastically reduced (from 300% to approximately 30-40%) after two growing seasons. [92] (dis) Similarly, the shortest size class showed the greatest increase in total root mass (four-time increase from initial conditions), nearly doubling the increase in root mass observed in the medium and tall size class (2.2-2.5 times greater after two years). [93] (dis) Reduced growth response differences driven by morphological characteristics had previously been observed in aspen on less stressful sites (Landhäusser et al. 2012b). [94] (dis) The lack of competition was likely the main driver of aspen growth response on the Mulch site, as the soil conditions appeared to be generally more favorable in the Plow and Grass sites (i.e. lower bulk density and higher soil nutrient concentrations, see Appendix 2). [95] (dis) On the Ag-field site; however, where competition was also low and the moisture deficit was high ((#page-5-0)a)), tall seedlings did not grow substantially in height (less than 25 cm over 2 years) compared to the two shorter size classes. [96] (dis) In this situation, tall size class seedlings had the greatest quantity of leaf area to maintain ((#page-8-0)) with the lowest relative root mass, potentially placing it at greatest risk of drought and further emphasizing that moisture stress can have as much of an impact on seedling development as competing vegetation. [97] (dis) This result also highlights the potential drawback of using taller aspen seedlings where moisture may be an environmental constraint. [98] (dis) On sites where significant competition was present from the onset of outplanting (Grass and Gravel-pit sites), size played less of a role in the growth and establishment of aspen. [99] (dis) The abundance of root competition in the Grass site or the very dry conditions at the Gravel-pit diminished the benefit of a high root-to-shoot ratio and all seedlings performed poorly. [100] (dis) The presence of competing roots has been associated with limiting resource uptake in newly planted seedlings, but has also been associated with other effects such as allelopathy (Landhäusser and Lieffers 1998). [101] (dis) Principally, a seedling stock type capable of enhanced root growth should be beneficial on sites with significant belowground competition. [102] (dis) However, tall size class seedlings which had the greatest total root growth, did not appear to benefit from this response in our study over the short-term. [103] (dis) This may have been attributable to the type of root system development, as the tall seedlings grew relatively fewer roots from the plug into the surrounding soil (Figure 5 (d)). [104] (dis) Root egress was an important growth parameter in our study as shorter size class seedlings with increased egress showed greater first year height growth. [105] (dis) Increased root egress should also lead to better soil plant contact making these seedlings likely better candidates in a competitive environment. [106] (dis) The reduced root egress observed in the taller size class could suggest that despite the increased root growth in larger seedlings, most root development did not occur outside of the existing root plug. [107] (dis) Similar results have been observed in lodgepole pine seedlings (Pinus contorta Douglas), where seedlings with a larger root mass showed reduced egress due to root binding. [108] (dis) Coupled with a lack of root egress, a taller shoot carrying more leaf mass ((#page-8-0)(a)) was detrimental for tall seedlings, which showed higher mortality at both sites and particularly at the Gravel-pit site during the dry conditions of 2015. [109] (dis) While initial seedling morphology can be tailored for drier site conditions to a certain extent (Pinto et al. 2011; Landhäusser et al. 2012b), there are physiological limitations within a given species where manipulation of seedling morphology is not sufficient and other species or selected drought tolerant genotypes may have to be used on these sites. [110] (dis) The methods of this study limit its ability to establish causal relationships between seedling size and outplanting performance in relation to site conditions, due to a lack of replication at the site level. [111] (dis) However, we successfully observed a general pattern in the effectiveness of a high root-to-shoot ratio for aspen seedlings, as short size class seedlings had greater two-year height growth over the tall size class on four of the six sites. [112] (dis) Additionally, observing similar growth responses between size classes at the Grass and Gravel-pit sites due to competition being present during outplanting highlights the importance of competition control, as extreme growing conditions will diminish any benefit of modified seedling characteristics. [113] (dis) By observing similar seedling responses between two study areas which exhibited a gradient of vegetation competition among the different sites, our study was effective in showing seedling establishment in response to seedling size over a wider range of site characteristics rather than narrowing in on one type of treatment. [114] (con) Contrary to seedling characteristic studies for other species, which recommend taller seedling stock when competing vegetation is present, there was not enough evidence from our study to recommend this approach for aspen. [115] (con) While the simultaneous influence of initial height and root-to-shoot ratio could not be separated in this study, taller seedlings were not competitive as they were limited by a lower root-to-shoot ratio. [116] (con) Tall seedlings with a high root-to-shoot ratio may be more competitive with competing vegetation; however, this must be balanced against overall production costs. [117] (con) Although we did not find substantive differences between short and medium seedlings, planting a short seedling (<46 cm height) in a competitive environment could pose risks in a longer time frame (3–5 years) if the seedling is not able to overtop competing vegetation (our study did not address this timeline). [118] (con) Our study did illustrate that short-term competition control was impactful and if this treatment had been maintained for an additional growing season it may have been a sufficient time period to allow seedlings from the short and medium-size classes to better tolerate or even suppress competing vegetation at this planting density. [119] (con) Improving site conditions plays a critical role for seedling establishment, as controlling competing vegetation will help to ensure successful seedling establishment. [120] (con) When competing vegetation is present, aspen seedlings will grow at a much slower rate, regardless of their initial size. [121] (con) Although climate factors cannot be controlled, differences in seedling development among the sites in our study show the importance of moisture availability on these boreal sites; therefore, creating site conditions that enhance root development and moisture availability may better facilitate establishment in dry years.
